site.name: Andy Keeley
site.role: CCO at a travel tech company · not a developer

intro:
I started using Claude Code in Feb-26. I work in a tech company, but i'm the commercial guy. I understand the ecosystem, but have never written a line of code.

Seven months later, there are sixteen things on this page. One runs my working week. One trades real money every day without asking me. One is a maths game my nine-year-olds actually ask to play. They were all built the same way: describe the problem properly, argue with the output until it's right, ship it, then keep using it until it breaks.

The hard part was never the code.

projects.name: mentor-agent
projects.description: The hub everything else plugs into. Runs my week on GTD and EOS — rocks, weekly scorecard, pipeline, reviews. Reads my calendar and inbox over MCP, holds context on every customer account, and has a Deal Prep mode I use before commercial negotiations. Six single-letter shell commands so capture never has a friction cost.

value.tip: genuinely can't work without it now

projects.name: investment-agent
projects.description: Autonomous trading agent. Scans the crypto market, scores candidates on momentum, sentiment, risk/reward and liquidity, sizes the position through a risk manager, executes on Kraken, and emails me a daily digest of what it did and why. The interesting part isn't the trading — it's the rules it can't talk itself out of: stop-loss set at entry, a hard cash floor, a maximum hold it has to re-underwrite. Runs unattended.

effort.tip: weekends and evenings over ~3 weeks, still tuning

value.tip: the discipline is worth more than the p&l

projects.name: zenbox
projects.description: Self-hosted email triage that replaced a paid SaneBox subscription. Gmail pushes new mail through Pub/Sub to a service that sorts it on rules I control — whitelist, greylist, am-I-actually-a-recipient, bulk-mail detection. Two independent instances, one per mailbox, sharing only the code. Plus a Chrome extension so I can change a sender's rule without leaving the inbox.

value.tip: cancelled the subscription, kept the quiet inbox

projects.name: customer-health-dashboard
projects.description: Reads CCO Hub exports and aged debt reports, weights them into a single health score across the whole customer portfolio, and renders a dashboard I can take straight into a board pack. Replaced a manual process that used to eat an afternoon.

projects.name: ar-collections-copilot
projects.description: Turns the weekly AR ledger into an execution-ready collections plan. Prioritises accounts on value and risk, drafts the chase, recommends the escalation path, and remembers every payment promise and whether it was kept. Deliberately advisory — it recommends, a human sends. Goal: 60-day debtor ratio from ~40% to under 10%.

value.tip: debt ratio moving the right way

projects.name: fitness-mentor
projects.description: My coach. Knows my training history, my weak points and every session I've logged. Five modes — log, review, plan, check, rehab. The bit I'm proudest of: before it does anything else it runs the arithmetic on my own data and tells me what's drifted — a skipped session, a stale flag, rehab that isn't going in, or a training block that quietly finished two weeks ago and I hadn't noticed. There's a phone app for logging sets at the rack, and it wrote the brief I took to my physio.

effort.tip: restructured twice as i worked out what i needed

value.tip: replaced a coach i was paying for

projects.name: health-tracker
projects.description: Correlates what I drink with what my body does about it — resting heart rate, HRV and sleep score, straight from Garmin. Dose-response curves, streak analysis, and the uncomfortable chart where the trend line meets the weekend. Guilt-as-a-service.

projects.name: maths-challenge
projects.description: Maths practice for my boys, disguised as a fighting game. Eight Key Stage 2 topics; each round is a match against an opponent with a health bar, a super meter that rewards streaks, and a rank stamp at the end. Nothing in it reads as losing — that was a design rule. There's a second area of trials modelled on their school's cognitive assessment. The save file has no reset button, on purpose: their history is the only record of what they've played, and the only input for tuning the difficulty.

effort.tip: the most iterated thing i've built

projects.name: anki-srs
projects.description: Spaced repetition built properly — SM-2 scheduling, four-button grading, and an append-only review log so I can swap the algorithm out later without losing history. Card types are pluggable, so one deck of famous paintings became decks for capitals, flags, US states, life philosophies and commercial fundamentals.

effort.tip: a weekend, then kept extending it

value.tip: the commercial deck earns its keep

projects.name: sonic-fighters
projects.description: A browser fighting game for my boys. Three.js, a physically-based rendering pipeline, a night arena and a broadcast-style HUD. Started as a weekend thing, then got rebuilt from the visuals up once they kept asking for more characters.

effort.tip: rebuilt once i knew what good looked like

projects.name: realm-raiders
projects.description: Split-screen 3D co-op adventure for two players on one laptop. Procedural low-poly island, camera-relative movement, terrain and obstacle collision, character abilities. Built in phases from a written spec — walking skeleton first, structured so combat and characters bolt on cleanly afterwards.

usage.tip: when we get a rainy afternoon

projects.name: beyblade-clash
projects.description: Two-to-three player Beyblade battle in the browser. Spin physics, collisions, stadium walls, hand-drawn bey art. Built in an evening because they asked.

projects.name: not-so-fast
projects.description: A Chrome extension that makes you earn access to distracting sites. Reach for the wrong tab and it puts a typing challenge in the way — long enough that the impulse has usually passed by the time you finish.

usage.tip: every time i reach for the wrong tab

projects.name: hotel-booking-app
projects.description: Full-stack booking app built on our Universal Hotel API — search, results, rooms, basket, book. Built to show our engineering team what Claude Code could do. Their reaction was the whole point.

effort.tip: my first real build, steep learning curve

value.tip: proved the concept to the team

projects.name: wordle-solver
projects.description: Wordle solver over the official NYT answer list. Feed it what you know and it suggests the guess that eliminates the most remaining possibilities. Deployed, so anyone can use it.

projects.name: fitness-tracker
projects.description: Workout logger with reusable templates and a rest timer, deployed on Render with Postgres behind it. My first database-backed web app, and where I learned what deploying actually involves. Now superseded by the logging app inside fitness-mentor.

value.tip: did its job, then got replaced

notes: I'm a CCO, not a developer. My background is commercial — ARR growth, account management, contract negotiations. I started building because I had problems nobody else was going to solve.

Every project here was built by describing what I wanted to Claude Code in plain English, iterating on the output, and deploying it. The stack listed on each card is what Claude Code chose, not what I specified.

The hard part was never the code. It's knowing which problem is actually worth solving, being specific about what 'done' looks like, and being honest when something isn't working and needs rebuilding. That's the same job I do commercially — it just has a terminal attached.
If you've got a problem that feels like it should be software but you don't have developers to build it — [get in touch](mailto:andy.keeley@gmail.com). I might be able to help.
